newsitem.title: GERMANY: German publishers see healthy market for CD-ROMs.
newsitem.headline: German publishers see healthy market for CD-ROMs.

text.p: Electronic publishing on CD-ROM is still a growing field in Germany and is at no risk of being superseded by the developing market for Internet book projects, industry experts said at the Frankfurt Book Fair.

Usable CD-ROMs, not flashy, functionless one-offs, will be key to wooing Germany's 8.5 million computer-owning households, experts said on Wednesday at the Fair which has fast evolved into the world's biggest venue for electronic publishing.

"We have all seen CD-ROM firms in the U.S. fade out of the market, but you have to ask yourself -- what kind of quality were they producing?" the German Federation of Book Publishers' electronic specialist Florian Langenscheidt told reporters.
"What we have now is a slowly maturing market with a clear process of selection in operation," he said.

German publishers have been forced to rethink their initial bullish forecasts for demand for CD-ROMs, which managed a retail sales volume of just 200 million marks in 1995, just two percent of retail publishing sales. Total German CD-ROM sales in the period were 720 million marks.

Experts say German buyers were disappointed that many early CD-ROMs had little practical use. The industry's first surprise hit and perennial best seller remains the mundane CD-ROM German telephone directory.

The Federation of Book Publishers is planning a major CD-ROM marketing push through December, with leading products -- especially reference works -- to go on display in about 500 retailers nationwide.
Between 2,000 and 2,500 German CD-ROMs are expected to be produced by the end of this year, up from 1,500 last year and 400 in 1994.

But the Federation is more sceptical about the fast developing market for Internet publishing, a significant focus at the week-long Book Fair which is to host the world's first auction of Internet publishing rights.

Federation official Bertram Gallus said he viewed Internet publishing "not with wholehearted enthusiasm" and urged tighter regulations to protect copyrights on systems which give almost unlimited access to end-users.

It was also unclear how publishers should value information made available over the Internet and, more importantly, how to charge for it. "Most Net surfers think they should get it all for free," Gallus said.

However Frank Steinhoff, managing director of the German unit of California-based PC software maker Adobe Systems Inc was more bullish, predicting that Germany would have about five million Net surfers by the end of 1998.
Not only print, but also television and film would be accessible over the Internet eventually, he said.

"The Internet is a growth phenomenon which nobody can ignore anymore," Steinhoff told a news conference. Once a print-weighted event,the Frankfurt Book Fair has developed in recent years into the world's biggest meeting for international electronic publishers, hosting 500 exhibits by specialist houses and 1,500 electronic displays by traditional print publishers.
